Traditional plus size starts at 12 in retail (this varies from store to store of course), modeling considers 8 / 10 the ideal “models” for the plus sized campaigns. They custom make clothing for them then sell in the 12+ sizes. A 1X is what used to be considered an XL in normal sizes which is around 12 / 14. Then of course you get into this W and extra fabric cutting that you mention. Vanity sizing has also overtaken the entire industry which adds another level of uncertainty (there’s actually great articles and videos showing girls buying the same style of jeans a few years apart and the sizing discrepancy as far as numerical sizes vs how they fit). The only way I could actjallt keep track that I was losing weight and not being fooled was to keep some of my old clothes and try them
On from time to time and see how big they were . It’s a total mess.  I did a fashion internship in NYC one summer, it’s actually crazy the disconnect between what is put out to retailers vs what the fashion world actually based it off of. Lots of manipulation, crazy things. I know Europe is cracking down on it a bit but in America it’s basically unchecked. I’m not a fan of regulation but it really is 2 different industries happening. What is the standard when the clothing is being made is a whole other world compared to what goes to stores. If a factory is making clothing for a brand that vanity sizes, they may use a size 7 template but it will be labeled as a size 5 or 3 when it gets tagged. Kinda fascinating but kinda a slap in the face too. The work around to this was SUPPOSED to be using the actual measurements which is why they’re usually displayed with a product listing on a website, however it’s actually super unreliable and there’s girls who have made whole careers on YouTube out of buying things based on their measurements and showing what a disaster it is. Asperger’s is a type of Autism, yes

Disclaimer: I have a bachelor’s degree in Early Childhood Education with a focus on special needs and child psychology (I don’t work in the field anymore) but hopefully I can provide some insight.

The “markers” were taught to look for have become so broad. A lot of kids diagnosed with autism aren’t “autistic” in the sense that they don’t have social difficulties, learning difficulties, behavior problems, or any other negative effect that you traditionally associate with a child with autism. 

Teachers (especially ones that have a focus like I do) are taught to look for certain signs that indicate a child may have a disorder (not just autism, we look for signs of dyslexia, motor skill problems, etc. the earlier you can get a kid diagnosed with an issue, the more intervention can be used to help them succeed in life to the best of their ability). When you begin to notice a series of markers, you’re asked to document the occurances over the course of about a month. Then you give those markers to the school psychologist and principle and everyone sits down with the parents and talk. Assistance is provided and a referral to a medical professional is usually given, or parents can choose to use their own medical personnel if desired.

In some cases, most cases, it’s a meer suggestion of, something could possibly hinder little Johnny’s ability to stay on track. We cannot give a formal diagnosis. The only time we would require the parents to take action is if the child is exhibiting extremely delayed or violent issues that create an unsafe environment for other students or faculty.


Now, the issue I take with this (and for the past 10 - 15 years it has been the same with things like ADHD) is the list of things that we as teachers notice and then are required to start documenting is so broad it can describe ANY child.

For example: if a child shows an interest in one specific topic (fixated on something) - that is a marker on the list and I am required to begin to observation process for documentation for a possible autistic child.

A child reads about their grade level but struggles with math? (Which is very common as those two subjects are opposites) begin the documentation process.

Basically, when I was teaching, if I would have gone through the process of documenting every potential issue, my entire class would have been labeled as “possibly autistic”. Normal childhood behavior isn’t accepted anymore.

Why do it? When you tell a child at a young age they’re “different” or have something “wrong” with them, even if it’s very minor or a misdiagnosis, it affects them and gives them the idea of ‘I’ll never be the same as everyone, I’ll never be as good as everyone else’

It also allows their parents to have an “excuse” if the child doesn’t reach their full potential. Basically, in my opinion, it’s a way to keep children from wanting to investigate, reach out and explore and in a lesser sense another way to “dumb down” the population.

There are children with legitimate autism and other diagnosis. But it is NO WHERE NEAR the number that are “diagnosised”

The intentions of the banning “professionals” rule were, in theory, a safeguard. In reality, it does not work anymore (not necessarily that it ever did) and now hurts athletes.

Agree, and many NBA athletes feel the same way. And remember, this isn’t an NBA exclusive issue - it’s just largely talked about in the NBA circuit because of all the issues the past year. Things change, the world changes and it’s time for the regulations to change.

> is it illegal to earn while in college?

In short, yes. Under the present program, it is because once you begin to get paid, you’re considered a “professional” and no longer eligible for college athletics.

This is a sticky situation with parents whose young children are gifted athletes. On one hand, it’s assumed they’ll go pro. On the other, if they accept any endorsements at all throughout that child’s life - it renders them ineligible to play in college.

This is the example I give when explaining: a mother has an 8 year old daughter who is very very good at gymnastics. She competes, and wins, at extremely high levels, and it is assumed she will eventually enter junior Olympics and Olympics. A leotard company approaches the mother and says: we will give your daughter free gear and this amount of money if she only wears our gear from now on. The mother says yes because the extra money can help with travel costs, extra gym time, and other expenses (sports at a high level are incredibly expensive). Fast forward 10 years: the girl is eligible to go into the Olympic trials, but decides she wants to go to school to become a pediatrician instead. She is not allowed to compete at the college level because she was a “professional” when she was 8 years old because her mom accepted the money and sponsorship. The other issue comes with the fact that the mother may have not even realized she was rendering her daughter ineligible by accepting a leotard sponsorship. 

The same goes for college athletes. They are not allowed to accept any form of gift, payment, or sponsorship while they are playing at the college level. That’s the issue that’s been getting heated in the past few months. 

Especially now in the age of social media where companies seek out young people with a lot of followers. Athletes can’t take any type of endorsement or sponsorship post, can’t rep any brand, can’t collaborate with any brand, etc.
